title: Knowledge check — 8 questions
note: Unlocks after the applied activity is submitted. Retakes are free and unlimited.

questions.prompt: What is the trust asymmetry this module describes?
options: That employees trust AI more than candidates do

That the function carrying the consequences of AI decisions about people is frequently absent from making them — 26% candidate trust against HR having no direct involvement in AI strategy in 52% of organizations
That executives overestimate how much employees trust automated processes
That trust in AI varies more by seniority than by function
questions.explanation: The systems spending employee and candidate trust are increasingly chosen by people who don't carry the consequence of spending it.

questions.prompt: Which candidate-trust figure is behavioural rather than attitudinal? `[V]`
options: That 26% trust AI to evaluate them fairly
That 79% want to be told when AI is used
That approximately 38% have walked away from a hiring process because it included an AI interview
All three are self-reported attitudes
questions.explanation: People aren't registering discomfort in a survey. They are leaving. That is the figure with a business consequence attached.

questions.prompt: What is the correct current statement of the EU position? `[V]`
options: The whole regime was deferred to December 2027, so nothing binds until then

High-risk employment obligations moved to 2 December 2027, but AI literacy and the emotion-recognition prohibition have bound since February 2025 and transparency obligations since 2 August 2026 — which puts a recruiting or HR chatbot in scope now
All obligations took effect 2 August 2026 as originally scheduled
Only systems making fully automated decisions are covered
questions.explanation: Deferral of one regime isn't runway across the Act, and a learner who takes away only the 2027 date has the dangerous version of this lesson.

questions.prompt: Why does the module recommend building a posture on a principle rather than the current statute? `[V]`
options: Because statutes vary too much between jurisdictions to build a single posture

Because statutory positions have moved twice in eighteen months in both directions, so a posture built on a date expires — while "AI is never the decision-maker" is stricter than most current law and will not need rewriting
Because principles are easier to communicate to employees than legal requirements
Because regulators give credit for principles-based compliance
questions.explanation: Being stricter than the law is exactly what makes it durable. You won't have to rewrite it when the law moves again, and it has moved twice already.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes having a policy from having governance?
options: Whether the policy was approved at board level
Whether the policy is reviewed on a defined cycle
Whether anything has ever been refused — a policy never enforced against someone with standing is a statement of intent, not a control
Whether the policy covers vendor systems as well as internal ones
questions.explanation: Writing the policy is operating-system work; refusing a peer's exception is governance. The one-minute diagnostic: when did your organization last say no to an AI deployment, and who was told?

questions.prompt: Roughly what proportion of organizations have an AI policy their own people consider clear and durable? `[V]`
options: About half
About one in three
About one in eight — roughly 49% have a policy, and about a quarter of those believe it is clear and durable
About one in twenty
questions.explanation: The rest have either nothing or a document. The multiplication is what makes the gap visible; either figure alone reads much better than the position actually is.

questions.prompt: What does the module say is the failure in the AI-coaching disclosure scenario?
options: Deploying a coaching tool without confidentiality guarantees
Failing to build an escalation path into the tool
That nobody has made a decision at all — so the behaviour is determined by the vendor's default rather than by the organization
Not informing employees that the tool retains conversation data
questions.explanation: Every available position is uncomfortable and the module doesn't claim to settle it. What it requires is a deliberate decision, written down and disclosed: B is one legitimate choice among several, not the answer.

questions.prompt: A learner searches thoroughly and can't find an unreviewed decision. How should that be scored?
options: As incomplete, since the activity requires a named system
As full credit if they submit the search — where they looked, who they asked, what they concluded — and especially if the reason is that nobody could tell them what systems are running
As evidence their organization has mature AI governance
As a reason to complete the activity using a hypothetical system
questions.explanation: The inability to see the systems is a larger finding than any single system would have been, and C is exactly the wrong inference, not finding one may mean there isn't one, or it may mean you can't see them, and the search is what distinguishes those.
